description.description_long:
An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, described President Donald Trump’s and senior officials’ public communications during the first days of the Iran war. Trump released prerecorded statements on Truth Social, spoke by telephone with more than a dozen journalists and discussed the attack before a White House ceremony without taking questions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine held a Pentagon briefing. AP reported that the administration’s explanations drew criticism and described limits on which reporters were called on during briefings.

These reported events support an account of communications choices and press-access disputes surrounding the war. They do not establish that the administration turned support for military action into a test of personal loyalty, or that the public discussion was deliberately organized as a domestic identity campaign. The narrower description retains the documented media and communications issues without assigning an unverified political strategy.
description.description_medium: AP described the Trump administration’s communications about the Iran war as unconventional and reported criticism of the explanations and press access. The account includes prerecorded statements, telephone interviews, remarks before a White House ceremony without questions and a Pentagon briefing where major outlets were not called on. These events support scrutiny of how the administration presented the war. The report does not document a loyalty test or show that support for the strikes was made a proxy for personal loyalty.

description.description_long: The Associated Press reported on December 20, 2025, that at least 16 files had disappeared from the Justice Department’s public Epstein-records webpage less than a day after being posted. One missing image showed a drawer containing photographs, including one of Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell. The department had not explained the disappearance at the time of AP’s report and said it was continuing to review and redact materials. Reuters reported the next day that DOJ restored the Trump photo after officials determined that no Epstein victims appeared in it. This later action adds a documented outcome to the initial report: the photo was reposted after review. It does not establish who directed the removal of every file, whether the other files were restored for the same reason, or that the episode caused a lasting change in public assessments of Trump’s transparency claims. The supported account is a temporary disappearance and restoration of the identified photo, with the department’s stated review rationale.

It says that this focus kept Trump’s transparency claims vulnerable to procedural criticism, because access mechanics can shape credibility more directly than rhetoric alone.

The notes do not identify the specific records sought, the exact access procedures or restrictions described, or the parties responsible for particular disclosure decisions. The Guardian source is linked as reporting on the disclosure conflict, but its contents have not been independently reviewed for this entry.

The supported consequence is reputational and procedural: when a transparency claim is assessed alongside obstacles to access, the claim may remain open to criticism even if officials publicly emphasize openness. The supplied material does not establish that information was unlawfully withheld, resolve the underlying disclosure dispute, or document a formal finding of misconduct. description.description_long:
The Guardian reported on February 26, 2026, that it had obtained three FBI Form 302 memoranda memorializing 25 pages of agents’ notes from four interviews conducted in 2019. The Justice Department had not included those records when it uploaded millions of Epstein-related files. The Guardian described the records as containing an explicit allegation against Donald Trump, but emphasized that it was unsubstantiated and unverified; the FBI brought no charges related to the claim, and Trump has denied wrongdoing.

The report said only the first interview was in the public release, and that interview did not name Trump. An administration official confirmed the missing reports were authentic and told the Guardian the department considered the files duplicative and not legally required to be released. The DOJ also told NPR that nothing had been deleted and withheld records were duplicative or privileged. Congressional Democrats sought an accounting, and the Republican oversight chair said lawmakers would examine the matter. The reporting documents a dispute about specific records and the department’s release process; it does not establish why the records were omitted or validate the allegation.

description.description_long: In an article published April 1, 2026, The Guardian reported that Trump had said over the preceding weekend that he wanted to 'take the oil in Iran' by seizing a key export hub. The article pointed to Kharg Island, Iran's main oil-export terminal, and noted that Trump had voiced interest in taking foreign oil for more than a decade. Experts quoted in the story characterized that rhetoric as reflecting a belief that the United States was entitled to resources it wanted, describing the approach as 'fossil-fuel imperialism.' This was their interpretation of Trump's statements and history. The article connected the remark to the Iran war but did not establish that acquiring oil was the conflict's sole purpose, that a seizure had occurred, or that U.S. forces had orders to occupy Kharg Island. The episode records explicit resource language in a conflict otherwise discussed in security terms.
description.description_medium: The Guardian laid out how Trump's appetite for Iranian oil fit a much older pattern of fossil-fuel imperial thinking, the belief that the United States is entitled to resources it covets. That matters because it helps explain the greed lurking under the posture. The war was sold in security language, but the underlying imagination kept sounding like a burglar with a flag pin.

It also supplies no evidence connecting Donald Trump to the investigation. The event is therefore the scrutiny of Russian money flows through a major U.S. bank and the questions raised about who owned or controlled accounts, not a Trump business or campaign action. The distinction matters because the original title placed “Trump” before a banking story without documenting his involvement. description.description_long: On 21 May 2026, NOAA issued an Atlantic hurricane-season outlook that gave a 55 percent chance of below-average activity. The agency forecast eight to 14 named storms, including three to six hurricanes and one to three major hurricanes; a typical season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes. Forecasters attributed the lower outlook in part to a likely El Niño, which increases wind shear that can suppress storm development in the Atlantic. NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs said there was a high probability of El Niño forming, but the outlook remained probabilistic: it did not promise a storm-free season. AP noted that even a less active season can include a devastating landfall, and that El Niño has less influence on Gulf Coast landfalls than Atlantic activity overall. A seasonal forecast describes expected storm frequency, not the government’s ability to prepare for a specific hurricane. That distinction matters amid separate concerns about staffing and readiness; the weather outlook alone cannot answer those operational questions.

description.description_long: The Justice Department announced federal charges against Hunter Biden on June 20, 2023: two misdemeanor counts for failing to pay taxes and a felony firearm count. Prosecutors said he had agreed to plead guilty to the tax offenses and enter a diversion agreement on the gun charge. House Republicans criticized that proposed resolution as preferential treatment and alleged interference in the investigation. The agreement did not take effect as announced: at a July 26 hearing, Judge Maryellen Noreika questioned its structure and the parties left without an accepted plea. In August, Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed U.S. Attorney David Weiss as special counsel over the investigation and related prosecutions. Weiss later told lawmakers he had full authority and had not been overruled by other Justice Department officials. These events document both a federal prosecution and a political dispute over its handling. The charges alone neither prove nor disprove broader claims of DOJ weaponization, and the record cited here does not establish that President Joe Biden directed charging decisions.
description.description_medium: Throughout 2023, Trump and Republicans relentlessly promoted the false claim that the DOJ was weaponized against Republicans while protecting Hunter Biden. The claim was undercut when Hunter Biden was charged with federal gun crimes and tax evasion. Despite months of House Republican investigations, no evidence emerged of Biden directing DOJ decisions. The disinformation campaign was designed to delegitimize Trump prosecutions by false equivalence and manufactured outrage.

description.description_long:
Attorney General Pam Bondi oversaw Justice Department decisions that dismissed charges or offered favorable plea deals to some Trump allies while opening or reopening investigations involving Democratic officials, journalists, and former prosecutors who had investigated Trump. The pattern emerged during Bondi’s first months as attorney general.

Career prosecutors documented receiving direction to consider the White House’s political preferences in charging decisions. Several resigned, saying they could not carry out their duties free from political interference. Former attorneys general from both parties condemned the department’s direction as an extreme politicization of federal law enforcement.

Prosecutors have discretion to bring or dismiss cases based on evidence and law, but political direction can undermine public confidence in equal treatment. The reported dismissals and investigations raised concern that the department was protecting allies while targeting opponents. The individual cases had different facts, but the broader pattern put the independence of federal prosecutors and the credibility of the Justice Department under scrutiny.

Career prosecutors reportedly received direction to consider White House preferences. description.description_long: On August 21, 2026, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin released a Democratic staff report titled “Pardons, Inc.” The report estimated that Trump’s pardons and commutations had erased nearly $1.7 billion in restitution, fines and forfeitures owed to victims and taxpayers. It argued that some wealthy white-collar offenders and drug traffickers obtained clemency through intermediaries connected to Trump’s political circle or family business interests. The report’s dollar figure is a committee-staff estimate based on identified cases, not a court-ordered accounting of every pardon. Separately, The Independent reported that at least 97 people pardoned for January 6-related offenses had later been arrested, charged or convicted of other crimes. It also described the case of Jon Ponder, a bank robber pardoned by Trump in 2020 who was arrested in 2026 and faced 20 charges, including sexual assault and unauthorized contact with incarcerated women. Those were allegations in a criminal case, not convictions. The later arrests are distinct from the committee report’s financial estimate and do not prove that every clemency recipient reoffended. Together, the reports raised questions about the effects of broad clemency and whether private relationships shaped access to the pardon process. The allegations about a “cash-for-clemency” system remain the report authors’ conclusions and are not presented as judicial findings.
description.description_medium: On August 21, 2026, House Judiciary Committee Democrats released a staff report estimating that Trump’s pardons and commutations erased nearly $1.7 billion in restitution, fines and forfeitures owed to victims and taxpayers. The report alleged that wealthy applicants used Trump-connected intermediaries and financial ties to secure clemency. Separately, The Independent reported that nearly 100 people pardoned for January 6 offenses later faced charges or arrests for other crimes, including pardoned nonprofit leader Jon Ponder. These are committee and news-report claims; charges are not convictions.
